title: Theories of Minds: The Drive for Identity and Good Relationships

html: The preceding sections have treated the environment as if it were composed primarily of physical objects whose dynamics, while complex, are governed by stable causal laws amenable to compression and control. But the single most consequential feature of the human ecological niche is that it is saturated with other agents–entities whose behavior is generated by hidden generative models of approximately the same complexity as the observer’s own. Other agents are unique among environmental dynamics in being simultaneously (i) the highest-dimensional prediction targets (their behavior is driven by beliefs, desires, emotions, plans, and social commitments that are only partially observable), (ii) the most non-stationary (they learn, deceive, update, and strategically adapt to the observer’s own actions), and (iii) the highest-stakes (they are the primary source of both the greatest fitness benefits–cooperation, mating, alloparental care, coalition defense, cultural knowledge transfer–and the greatest fitness costs–aggression, exclusion, exploitation, reputational destruction). This convergence of inferential difficulty and fitness relevance means that natural selection has imposed enormous pressure on human brains to build, maintain, and deploy rich generative models of other minds–and, reflexively, a generative model of one’s own mind as it appears to other minds. The result is a suite of social-cognitive capacities (mentalizing, empathy, reputation management, norm internalization, identity construction) that are not epiphenomenal add-ons to a fundamentally asocial optimization engine but constitute a superordinate objective in their own right: the drive to maintain accurate, predictive models of the social world and to occupy a viable position within it.
